<reason>Both sides argued at a high level, but CON (Side B) built the cleaner decision rule and kept narrowing the clash. B's "portable vs. sits with the building" frame and later "asymmetry of default" gave the judge a concrete mechanism to weigh, whereas PRO's case rested on retrospective institutional review that B repeatedly showed gets deferred, merged, or renamed. B caught a real contradiction (PRO's "perpetual boom-bust" complaint vs. its later claim that competition "has never closed anything"), neutralized PRO's one closure example (Mill Hill as relocation), and exploited PRO's concession that "nothing, prospectively" stops a director favoring protégés. PRO's strongest moves—the Karikó boomerang, "grant panels are the building at field scale," and "a lottery is an obituary for competition"—were sharp and genuinely pressured B, and the treadmill-tax point was never fully dismantled. But B's closing turned PRO's own line ("a default cannot tell a dead lab from a daring one") into "neither can a director," and reframed the question as what happens after a wrong judge—a comparison PRO never squarely answered. B made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 (A2) on non-renewal: it answered PRO's pressure question directly, exposed the boom-bust/"never closed anything" contradiction, reduced Mill Hill to "money changed postcode," and crystallized the "asymmetry of default" that PRO's closing had to fight on B's terms.</best_rebuttal>
